note: Single-pass extraction by Claude reading the paper text; evidence references sections/figures/tables. No multi-run validation.

components.description: Encoded absences: definition, mechanism, failure of standard XAI, adapted methods and empirical findings

nodes.name: Standard XAI ties activation to presence
nodes.description: Mainstream attribution and feature-visualization methods associate neuron activation with the presence of concepts: attribution highlights present input features and feature visualization finds inputs that maximize activation.

nodes.name: Encoded absence defined
nodes.description: A neuron z_j encodes the absence of a concept if inserting the concept into the input decreases its activation, i.e. f_j([x,C=1]) < f_j([x,C=0]) (Definition 2.1).

nodes.name: DNNs can implement encoded absences
nodes.description: A neuron encoding the absence of a concept can be constructed with negative weights from neurons encoding its presence plus a source of positive potential, so DNNs can implement such neurons (Proposition 2.2).

nodes.name: Target attribution misses absences
nodes.description: Standard target attribution only highlights concepts present in the input, and concepts whose absence is informative are typically not present in images of the target class, so they cannot appear.

nodes.name: Maximization cannot visualize absences
nodes.description: Feature visualization through maximization cannot visualize concepts whose absence is encoded, since maximally activating inputs contain minimal amounts of inhibiting concepts.

nodes.name: Counterfactual explanations cannot explain absences
nodes.description: Counterfactual explanations operate between samples or classes and implicitly delete content, so they cannot tell whether a prediction relies on presence of a class concept or absence of a competing one.

nodes.name: Non-target attribution
nodes.description: Computing the attribution for class t on inputs from other classes (non-target attribution) makes concepts whose absence is informative appear, with negative attribution indicating inhibition.

nodes.name: Feature visualization through minimization
nodes.description: Finding the input that minimizes a neuron's pre-activation reveals the patterns that inhibit it, i.e. the concepts whose absence the neuron encodes.

nodes.name: Hassenstein-Reichardt toy model: standard XAI fails
nodes.description: In a synthetic Hassenstein-Reichardt detector, Integrated Gradients and highest-activating patches explain the neuron encoding both directions faithfully but only highlight the left-to-right motion for the neuron encoding presence of one direction and absence of the other.

nodes.name: Non-target attribution reveals the HR absence
nodes.description: The proposed modifications reveal the missing inhibitory signal in the Hassenstein-Reichardt detector, with right-to-left motion receiving negative attribution (Fig 3e).

nodes.name: Trained toy CNN learns an encoded absence
nodes.description: A small CNN trained to classify green-pixel presence learns an output that encodes absence of green via a negative weight from the green channel and a positive weight from the red/blue channel, matching the mechanistic construction.

nodes.name: Adapted methods explain the toy CNN
nodes.description: On the toy CNN, standard methods fail to show the green pixel's causal role, while non-target attribution and minimization highlight the green pixel for the absence-encoding output (Fig 4).

nodes.name: ImageNet models use encoded absences
nodes.description: In VGG19, ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16, inserting least-activating patches strongly suppresses channel activations while random patches have little effect (Table 1).

nodes.name: Other concept-discovery notions don't capture absences
nodes.description: Inserting logical-NOT patches from Mu and Andreas (2020) or the most activating patches decreases activation no more than random patches, so they target presences or a different notion of NOT.

nodes.name: Absences support fine-grained classification
nodes.description: Channels that encode presence of concepts of a class often simultaneously encode absence of concepts of closely related classes, e.g. Border Collie vs. Leonberger, aiding fine-grained discrimination and robustness (Fig 6).

nodes.name: Biased model overfits to colorful patches
nodes.description: On a synthetic ISIC bias where all benign samples have colorful patches, a model with no debiasing overfits to them and fails when the patches are absent or the association is inverted (Table 2).

nodes.name: Presence-only debiasing is insufficient
nodes.description: Presence debiasing with existing attribution priors reduces the bias but still fails on malignant samples with inserted patches, indicating bias from the absence of colorful patches.

nodes.name: Presence+absence debiasing works
nodes.description: Presence+absence debiasing gives the highest average accuracy in both setups without the training bias, comparable to a model trained without bias (Table 2).

nodes.name: Biases arise from absence too
nodes.description: Biases can arise from concept absence as well as presence, so effective debiasing must account for both.

isolated_nodes.name: Absences matter in biology
isolated_nodes.description: In biological systems, absences serve as reasoning cues, e.g. the Hassenstein-Reichardt model has Drosophila neurons activated by rightward motion in combination with absence of leftward motion.

isolated_nodes.name: Non-target attribution has noise caveat
isolated_nodes.description: Negative non-target attributions do not by themselves guarantee an encoded absence because attribution can be noisy, though this did not meaningfully affect the studied applications.

isolated_nodes.name: Non-target attribution resembles targeted FGSM
isolated_nodes.description: Non-target attribution is algorithmically similar to the input gradient with respect to a non-true class used in targeted FGSM attacks.

structural_reasoning: Argument runs from the definition and mechanism of encoded absences, through why standard XAI misses them and the proposed adaptations, to toy and ImageNet evidence and the debiasing application.
